title: POC scoping: deployment economics & SLA discussion - Amaris Health
topics: Workload sizing and typical traffic patterns
Benchmark plan and metrics (latency, throughput, cost)
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
summary: Discovery + POC scoping focused on deployment economics and SLA tradeoffs for Amaris Health. Customer wants a short pilot to validate latency SLOs and cost per request for a clinical summarization feature. Key concerns: PHI handling, regional data residency, ability to pin model versions, and predictable throughput for morning batch window. Next steps: Redwood to run a 72-hour benchmark with customer sample prompts, share security pack and pricing options (hosted vs dedicated), schedule follow-up architecture deep dive next week.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Alvarez (SE remote), Ava Kim (CSM) / Liam O'Connor (Amaris Head of ML), Sara Mehta (Eng Manager), Noah Ruiz (Security), Daniel Park (Infra), Marta Lopez (Product)

Summary (auto): quick alignment on POC goals, workload shape and security gating; decision drivers are latency SLO, cost predictability, and data residency.

[00:00] Ethan Park: okay everyone thanks for joining, we wanna make sure we align on what success looks like for a pilot, I'm gonna hand over to Priya to frame the benchmark approach, but first can you confirm the primary use case?
[00:08] Liam O'Connor: yeah, the primary is clinical note summarization and triage for our ambulatory clinics, it's PHI yes, so governance matters. Typical request length is 1500-2k tokens, output 200-400 tokens. Peak window 8-10AM local, about 120-180 qps across clusters but most requests are single-user synchronous.
[00:25] Priya Singh: got it, thanks Liam. so latency SLOs? do you have a target p95 or p99 that will be considered successful?
[00:33] Sara Mehta: target p95 around 800ms ideally, p50 should be sub-200ms, but we can be flexible if cost tradeoffs are clear. for initial pilot we care more about p95 under load.
[00:45] Priya Singh: understood. for hosted vs dedicated vs private, high level tradeoff: hosted is fastest to ship and easiest for burst, dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput/cost, private gives data residency and full control but longer lead time.
[01:02] Noah Ruiz: on the privacy side, we need SOC2 reports, customer-managed keys ideally, and audit logs for every inference. can hosted meet that or do we need private?
[01:12] Ethan Park: hosted offering supports BYOK via KMS integration in some regions; for full HSM-managed keys and air-gapped options you'd look at Private. we can surface detailed artifacts — Priya will send the security pack.
[01:24] Daniel Park: also we have networking constraints, we prefer VPC peering if possible, low egress cost, and route control. how do the dedicated and private networking models differ?
[01:33] Jordan Alvarez: dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools with private networking and optional VPC peering; Private gives you control plane inside your VPC or on-prem where needed. both support audit logs, but Private allows you to keep telemetry inside your environment.
[01:48] Ethan Park: quick question on throughput modeling: you said 120-180 qps at peak and longer tokens. what's your expected average tokens per request across the day?
[01:57] Liam O'Connor: average about 700 tokens per call, but those morning surges skew higher. batch jobs will also run overnight at low priority.
[02:07] Priya Singh: for sizing a dedicated pool we typically assume concurrent inference capacity. with 700 tokens avg and concurrency ~200 we'd look at starting with 4 x H100-equivalent nodes for p95 800ms ballpark; if you want <400ms p95 you'd be in 8 x H100 space or use aggressive quantization and caching.
[02:28] Sara Mehta: can you quantify cost ballpark? we need to justify to finance.
[02:33] Ethan Park: rough order: hosted on our curated model ~ $X per 1M tokens (redacted in call notes) for generation; dedicated reserved capacity amortizes to Y/month for 4-node baseline; private has license and infra uplift plus deployment cost. we'll send detailed pricing scenarios.
[02:49] Marta Lopez: what about model pinning and rollouts? we want the ability to pin a model version and canary rollouts to a subset of traffic.
[02:57] Priya Singh: yes, Redwood supports model pinning and controlled rollouts with automatic fallback to a compatible variant. during the pilot we can set up canary at 10% traffic and monitor quality regressions.
[03:06] Noah Ruiz: for compliance we need retention rules, can we set per-customer retention and deletion?
[03:12] Jordan Alvarez: yes, retention TTLs can be configured per-account; Private gives you the strongest guarantee since data never leaves your VPC unless you opt-in. Hosted supports configurable retention and redaction options but audit of physical storage is limited to our SOC reports.
[03:27] Ethan Park: regarding benchmarks, plan we propose: 72-hour run, two phases: soak test (24h) at baseline load, peak assault windows simulated (several 1-hour ramps) and then cold-start/prefix caching effectiveness tests. we'll collect p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, KV cache hit rates, and failure/retry rates.
[03:47] Sara Mehta: that sounds reasonable. what telemetry will you give us? we need per-request traces and token-level cost breakout.
[03:53] Priya Singh: Redwood Console exposes per-route token breakdown, per-token cost trace, and we can share raw logs for the pilot if you need deeper analysis.
[04:03] Daniel Park: timeline? how quickly can we start the benchmark if we share samples and an access window?
[04:08] Ethan Park: once we have samples and basic account set up, we can spin up a hosted benchmark in 48 hours. dedicated proof-of-concept requires commit provisioning ~2-3 weeks lead mostly for capacity reservations; Private is 4-8 weeks depending on networking approvals.
[04:21] Marta Lopez: stakeholders for success: product-owner signoff on summary quality, infra signoff on latency/cost, and security signoff for PHI handling.
[04:29] Ethan Park: good — let's capture success criteria explicitly: (1) p95 latency under 800ms during peak with <=1% error rate, (2) cost per 1k tokens below threshold X (we'll propose scenarios), (3) ability to use BYOK or Private for PHI. if those met, we move to a 3-month pilot on dedicated.
[04:48] Liam O'Connor: that aligns, and we need a PO to finance dedicated if the numbers make sense.
[04:53] Priya Singh: quick gotcha — for long-context models you may need KV cache tuning; we'll recommend sequence-length-aware batching and prefix caching to reduce token costs. also quantization profiles might reduce memory footprint but will slightly affect quality; we'll include quality delta estimates in the report.
[05:10] Sara Mehta: any known limitations with function/tool-calling or structured output we should be aware of?
[05:16] Jordan Alvarez: function calling is supported; structured JSON outputs are stable but you should test against your evaluation set. we'll include a small harness to run deterministic evals during the benchmark.
[05:28] Ethan Park: ok wrapping up — next steps and owners as we outlined. anything else from the customer side?
[05:34] Noah Ruiz: please include explicit details about key rotation and audit log retention periods in the pack.
[05:38] Priya Singh: noted, we'll include KMS rotation policy options and audit retention defaults.
[05:44] Marta Lopez: can we do a short architecture call focusing only on Private feasibility next week? 30 minutes?
[05:48] Jordan Alvarez: yes I can do a 30-min slot, I'll propose times for week of 2026-03-23.
[05:53] Ethan Park: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and security attachments.
[05:57] Liam O'Connor: thanks, talk soon.

End transcript.
